query: For high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what testable methodological hypothesis could enable improved combinations of strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance? Explain why it should work, what measurable improvement is expected relative to the state of the art, the conditions under which it should or should not hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experimental result that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Systematic partial substitution of interstitial species (e.g., carbon or nitrogen) in a carefully balanced multicomponent (high-entropy) alloy will induce short-range order and/or nanoscale precipitates that simultaneously enhance yield strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture toughness beyond the levels attainable by the baseline compositions without interstitial additions.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or homogenized high-entropy alloy of Co–Cr–Ni or similar multi-principal element composition lacking intentional interstitial doping.
generation.intervention: Introduce low to moderate concentrations (≈0.5–1.0 at. %) of interstitial carbon or nitrogen through controlled melting and homogenization, followed by standard mechanical and microstructural characterization protocols (tension tests at room to elevated temperatures, fracture toughness measurements, etc.).
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing across a relevant range of temperatures and strain rates for structural applications, ensuring consistent processing routes (e.g., vacuum arc melting, homogenization treatments) to minimize confounding microstructural effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range chemical ordering and/or stabilized nanoprecipitates that refine the microstructure, reduce stacking fault energies, and promote beneficial dislocation and twinning interactions.
generation.mechanism: Interstitial additions locally modify lattice parameters and elemental discretization, creating short-range ordering that impedes dislocation movement in a controlled manner, promoting concurrent strengthening and ductility by activating multiple deformation pathways (e.g., partial dislocation slip and twinning) while maintaining high energy absorption.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped baseline alloy, at least a 10% increase in yield strength with minimal ductility loss (≤5%) and comparable or improved fracture toughness; Young’s modulus is expected to show moderate increases or remain comparable, supporting higher load-bearing capability.
generation.baseline: Current CrCoNi-based or similar HEAs/MEAs with typical yield strengths around 700–1000 MPa and ductility of 50–60%, as reported in known literature but without targeted interstitial additions.
generation.boundary: Excessive interstitial doping (beyond ~1 at. %) may lead to coarse carbides/nitrides and premature fracture; suboptimal heat treatments or incomplete homogenization could likewise degrade overall mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: Precise doping levels, processing routes, and alloy compositions must be optimized. Excess doping, competing secondary phases, or insufficient control of short-range ordering could reduce ductility or toughness.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare tensile and fracture toughness tests of baseline and interstitially doped HEA/MEA samples with systematically varied C or N contents (e.g., 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0 at. %). Use XRD, TEM, and atom probe tomography to confirm short-range order and/or precipitation states before and after mechanical deformation.
measurements: Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure at standard and elevated temperatures
Fracture toughness or crack growth resistance measurements (e.g., J-integral or KJc)
Atom probe tomography or microscopy evidence of short-range ordering or precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If interstitial substitution does not produce simultaneous improvement in both strength and toughness/ductility (e.g., improvement in one property is overshadowed by a substantial loss in the other), or if no measurable changes in short-range ordering/precipitation are detected, then the hypothesis is falsified.

These mechanical properties contradict the conventional inverse relationship between strength and ductility. Otto et al. Medium- and high-entropy alloys are an emerging class of materials that can exhibit outstanding combinations of strength and ductility for engineering applications. Computational simulations have suggested the presence of short-range order (SRO) in these alloys, and recent experimental evidence is also beginning to emerge. Unfortunately, the difficulty in quantifying the SRO under different heat treatment conditions has generated much debate on the atomic preferencing and implications of SRO on mechanical properties. Here we develop an approach to measure SRO using atom probe tomography. This method balances the limitations of atom probe tomography with the threshold values of SRO to map the regimes where the required atomistic neighbourhood information is preserved and where it is not. We demonstrate the method with a case study of the CoCrNi alloy and use this to monitor SRO changes induced by heat treatments. These species-specific SRO measurements enable the generation of computational simulations of atomic neighbourhood models that are equivalent to the experiment and can contribute to the further understanding and design of medium- and high-entropy alloys and other materials

AbstractDamage tolerance can be an elusive characteristic of structural materials requiring both high strength and ductility, properties that are often mutually exclusive. High-entropy alloys are of interest in this regard. Specifically, the single-phase CrMnFeCoNi alloy displays tensile strength levels of ∼1 GPa, excellent ductility (∼60–70%) and exceptional fracture toughness (KJIc>200 MPa√m). Here through the use of in situ straining in an aberration-corrected transmission electron microscope, we report on the salient atomistic to micro-scale mechanisms underlying the origin of these properties. We identify a synergy of multiple deformation mechanisms, rarely achieved in metallic alloys, which generates high strength, work hardening and ductility, including the easy motion of Shockley partials, their interactions to form stacking-fault parallelepipeds, and arrest at planar slip bands of undissociated dislocations. We further show that crack propagation is impeded by twinned, nanoscale bridges that form between the near-tip crack faces and delay fracture by shielding the crack tip. occupying_moves.lever: precise tuning of high-entropy alloy composition via targeted interstitial additions
occupying_moves.technique: vacuum arc melting and homogenization, followed by mechanical tests (tensile, hardness, fracture toughness) and microstructural characterization (SEM, TEM, XRD)
occupying_moves.conditions: room to elevated temperatures and relevant industrial strain rates for structural applications

chosen.lever: systematic partial substitution of interstitial species (e.g., C or N) to induce short-range order and precipitation
chosen.technique: precision alloy design, controlled melting, homogenization, and standard mechanical and microstructural tests
chosen.conditions: temperatures and loading rates representative of structural applications, with varied interstitial content
chosen.why: By carefully introducing interstitials (carbon or nitrogen) to high-entropy alloys in measured amounts, local chemical order and fine phases can be promoted, offering a proven route toward simultaneously enhancing strength, ductility, stiffness, and fracture resistance. Prior investigations on high- and medium-entropy alloys suggest that interstitial additions reduce stacking fault energies and refine microstructure, driving beneficial dislocation interactions and twinning. Experiments showing simultaneous improvements of ≥10% in yield strength with minimal (-5% or less) ductility loss, or a comparable improvement in fracture toughness, would demonstrate success. Conversely, if such interstitial adjustments fail to enhance multiple properties (e.g., yield strength gains but severe ductility loss), it would falsify the hypothesis that targeted interstitial composition control produces the sought mechanical synergy.
